appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte's marriage to Saint-Loup makes Swann's daughter "une Guermantes"; society people "qui n'avaient fait aucune attention à Gilberte" now stare at her with grave interest and ask to be presented to her fiancé, while she herself is convinced "que le nom de marquis de Saint-Loup était plus grand mille fois que celui de duc d'Orléans".
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage records a real and large rise in Gilberte's standing through the marriage, but frames the world's sudden attention — and Gilberte's own valuation of the name — with open irony.

appraisal_events.evidence: Adopted by M. de Charlus and given a Guermantes title, the tailor's niece marries into the Cambremer: "les rois épousaient les bergères"; the mother calls it "la récompense de la vertu", the narrator privately "le prix du vice, c'est un mariage à la fin d'un roman de Balzac".
appraisal_events.explanation: The girl is raised from Jupien's back-stairs relation to an adopted daughter of a near-royal house, an elevation the narration reports fully while ironizing the moral gloss placed on it.

appraisal_events.evidence: The mother's Combray acquaintances: "Vous savez ce que c'est que Mlle de Forcheville, c'est tout simplement Mlle Swann"; Charlus is "ce vieux qui entretenait déjà la mère... au vu et au su de Swann qui y trouvait son intérêt"; "je ne fréquenterai jamais la fille d'une femme qui a fait parler d'elle".
appraisal_events.explanation: Provincial gossip tries to strip the marriage of its lustre by dragging Gilberte back to her mother's past and her father's complaisance, but the narration quotes the tirade at satirical length and the mother contradicts it.

appraisal_events.evidence: "C'était beaucoup d'audace pour une femme tentée seulement par les cent millions qui lui fermaient les yeux sur le reste"; she retreats before the princesse de Silistrie's outcry, turns to Mlle d'Entragues, then "changea ses batteries, revint à Gilberte".
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes the mercenary calculation behind Mme de Marsantes' disinterested language and her rival's, and stages her public retreat and about-face as a small comedy of marriage-broking.

status_effects.explanation: Her standing visibly rises inside the world of the passage: people who had never noticed her now seek presentations and comment on the match.
The Guermantes boundary her father longed to see her cross is crossed: she becomes "une Guermantes" and will live at Tansonville as a Saint-Loup.
The Combray voices reduce her to "tout simplement Mlle Swann", the daughter of a kept woman with a doubtful bridegroom; the discredit registers even though the narration mocks its source.
Named for a Guermantes title and heir to Charlus's money, she is spoken of as belonging to a house the newspapers call "princes souverains".
The caste line of Combray is crossed: the niece of a man who would only have come up the service stairs enters the nobility by adoption and marriage.
The match anchors the Cambremer "dans ce clan des Guermantes où ils n'espéraient pas pouvoir jamais planter leur tente", and he now feels grand enough to consort with anyone.
She is the principal object of the gossip, counted through her lovers and denied any right to the name Forcheville.
The same voices make him a complaisant husband who profited from Charlus's keeping of Odette and who was not so rich as he seemed.
The narrator strips her disinterested praise of Gilberte down to the hundred millions and shows her yielding, veering, and returning without principle.
Her loud defence of the Faubourg is unmasked as a manoeuvre: "Elle n'avait crié qu'afin de se réserver Gilberte."

ambiguities: The Combray tirade is quoted at satirical length and contradicted by the mother, so how much of its discredit the narration lets stand against Gilberte, Odette, and Swann is left open.
